extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalists, policymakers, and news industry professionals
extracted.subtask_description: A Pew Research Center fact sheet summarizing measures and trends for high-traffic U.S. news websites, including audience metrics, digital outreach, social presence, and digital advertising revenue and market share. It compiles Comscore and eMarketer data and a Pew audit to provide longitudinal and cross-sectional snapshots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlet inclusion threshold (10 million average monthly unique visitors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news outlets included are those whose primary domain – the outlet’s flagship website – averaged at least 10 million unique visitors per month from October to December of each year analyzed, according to Comscore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes both digital-native and legacy outlets meeting the traffic level; 105 outlets met this threshold in 2022. See methodology for full list of domains and selection details. This threshold defines the "news outlets with the highest traffic" cohort used throughout the fact sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average fourth-quarter monthly unique visitors (Q4 avg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Average number of monthly unique visitors for the news outlets with the highest traffic (Q4 average for the year being analyzed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values reported by year (e.g., 2019–2022). Note: Q4 averages compared year-to-year; 2022 and 2021 cohort based on 2022 data. Source: Comscore Media Metrix® Multi-Platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average minutes per visit (visit duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Average minutes per visit for the news outlets with the highest traffic, reported as average minutes per visit by year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported annually (e.g., decline from about 1:50 in 2021 to about 1:45 in 2022). Source: Comscore Media Metrix® Multi-Platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: 'news outlets with the highest traffic'
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational definition used repeatedly: outlets that had a monthly average of at least 10 million unique visitors from October to December of the year being analyzed (primary domain analyzed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should interpret charts and percentages as applying to this defined cohort. Methodology note repeats this definition and points users to the methodology for domain lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile app availability by platform
rubrics_metrics.description: Share of high-traffic news outlets that have apps for iOS and Android, broken down as Android only, iOS only, or both platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example values: in 2023, Android+ iOS = 67%; iOS only = 6%; Android only = 2%. Data from a Pew Research Center audit of the 105 outlets; percentage of outlets without either type not shown. See audit methodology for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital outreach methods adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Percent of high-traffic outlets that use various digital outreach channels (newsletters, Flipboard, Apple News, podcasts, comments on articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: newsletters 92%; Flipboard 92%; Apple News 87%; podcasts 76%; comments 37% (2023 audit). Derived from a Pew audit of the 105 outlets; methodology describes site selection and audit process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media presence (platform-level adoption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Percent of high-traffic outlets with an official presence on specific social platforms (e.g., Facebook, X/Twitter, Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example values: Facebook 100%; X (Twitter) 99%; Instagram 97%; YouTube 93%; TikTok 89% (2023); Snapchat 25%. Notes: Twitter rebranded to X in 2023. Source: Pew Research Center audit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital advertising revenue totals and share of all advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual total digital advertising revenue in U.S. dollars (for all digital recipients, not just news) and its share of total advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: eMarketer estimates are used (e.g., $245 billion in 2022, comprising ~72% of all advertising). Note that figures are for all digital advertising, not solely news publishers; data from eMarketer U.S. Ad Spending Estimates, March 2023. Data for previous years are updated annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile advertising revenue totals and growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual mobile advertising revenue totals and growth over time, and mobile's share of digital advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mobile advertising increased from $146.1B (2021) to $161B (2022); mobile comprised ~66% of digital advertising revenue in 2022. Source: eMarketer estimates; note large growth since 2011.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital advertising revenue by device (desktop vs mobile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breakdown of annual digital advertising revenue between desktop digital advertising and mobile digital advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yearly tables provided (2011–2022). Note: digital advertising on CTV not shown. Data updated annually; source eMarketer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital display advertising revenue by device (desktop vs mobile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual digital display advertising revenue on desktop and mobile (display ads include banners, videos and other on-site ads), reported by year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data show mobile display rising faster than desktop; values reported in year-by-year tables. Note: data for years prior to 2017 may use different methodology (see 2018 archived fact sheet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital display advertising revenue by format
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual revenue for display ad formats: banner ads, sponsorship ads, video ads, and rich media other (interactive or audio/video components but not full video).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and trends: video ads were the largest segment in 2022 ($73.8B); banner ad revenue decreased in 2022. Table covers 2017–2022; earlier years use different methodology. Source: eMarketer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital display advertising market concentration by company
rubrics_metrics.description: Percent of annual digital display advertising revenue going to major companies (Meta, Google, Amazon, Twitter, etc.), reported by year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Meta 37% (2022), Google 10%, Amazon 6%; notes on corporate changes (Verizon/Yahoo/Oath/Apollo) and rebranding (Facebook→Meta). Numbers may not add to 100% due to rounding. Source: eMarketer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile digital display advertising revenue share by company
rubrics_metrics.description: Percent of annual mobile net digital display advertising revenue allocated to companies (Meta, Twitter, LinkedIn/Microsoft, Snapchat, Google, TikTok, Other) across years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Meta ~52% of mobile display in 2022; TikTok growing to ~5% in 2022. Table shows year-by-year shares; note corporate consolidation (LinkedIn under Microsoft) and rebranding. Source: eMarketer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal presentation and data availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Most metrics are presented as time series (annual tables and charts) and downloadable data (.csv) and images are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes indicate that data from previous years are updated annually and some longer-term series use different methodologies at earlier years (see archival notes). Download links (.csv) available for many tables and charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources, audit, and methodology transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary data sources used (Comscore Media Metrix® Multi-Platform for audience metrics; eMarketer U.S. Ad Spending Estimates for ad revenue; Pew Research Center audit for outreach and social presence) with links to methodology and archived fact sheets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodology notes specify selection criteria, audit procedures, and caveats (e.g., scope limited to primary domains, some data not shown like percent without apps). Users should consult methodology for domain lists and audit details; Pew lists staff who compiled the fact sheet and funding sources.
